about: Examples of the Etch simulator, per wafer. Each example has the same form as a preset saved with ☆ Save as my preset and exported: to add one, build it on the page, export it, and copy its "data" fields here (docs/DATA.md). Lengths in µm, angles in degrees from the flat, time in minutes; rate = key in etchants.json; fk = wafer frame (100, 110f, 110a, 111).

100.name: Cantilever along ⟨110⟩: released by convex-corner undercut
100.note: The beam edges run along ⟨110⟩, so {111} walls protect them; only the two convex corners at the free end are attacked by fast planes, and the undercut runs back along the beam until it is free (Lec 4-1 p. 8, Fig. 5c and 5d). Compare the next preset.

100.name: Cantilever along ⟨100⟩: released from its long edges
100.note: Edges along ⟨100⟩ have no {111} plane through them. In KOH they are undercut by near-vertical {100} planes at about R(100) (Pal & Sato pp. 246-248, condition c), so the beam is freed from the sides much sooner than the ⟨110⟩ beam.

100.name: Bridges: ⟨110⟩ bridge stays on a ridge, 45° bridge is released
100.note: A bridge along ⟨110⟩ has {111} walls on both edges and keeps a silicon ridge under it (Lec 4-1 p. 14 draws bridges over pits). The 45° (⟨100⟩) bridge has convex corners and ⟨100⟩ edges, so it is undercut and freed.

100.name: Mesa: convex-corner attack (no compensation)
100.note: Concave corners show the slowest plane, convex corners the fastest (Lec 4-1 p. 8). Read the undercut l and depth d from the readout: Ur = l/d is the input for compensation design (Pal & Sato p. 237). Pal & Sato report that a 90° convex corner in KOH turns into a 150 ± 2° corner (p. 235).

100.name: Mesa with ⟨110⟩-beam compensation
100.note: A beam along ⟨110⟩ is added at each convex corner (Lec 4-1 p. 9, Fig. 4.63; Pal & Sato pp. 243-245). Its length sets the depth at which the corner is reached: d = (0.5 W cos α + L sin α)/Ur (Pal & Sato p. 244). W = 40 µm and L = 110 µm here are design choices.

100.name: Mesa with ⟨100⟩-beam compensation (W = 2d)
100.note: A beam along ⟨100⟩ at each corner (Lec 4-1 p. 9, Fig. 4.64). Pal & Sato p. 249: the beam width should be twice the required etch depth, W = 2d; here W = 80 µm for d ≈ 40 µm (50 min at 0.797 µm/min). Beam length 180 µm is a design choice.

100.name: Mesa with square compensation
100.note: Squares centred on the convex corners (Pal & Sato pp. 241-243, Fig. 6.27). Pal & Sato report that the corners still bevel in KOH with this design. Square size 90 µm is a design choice.

100.name: Windows of different size and shape merging
100.note: Each window grows to the ⟨110⟩ rectangle that bounds it (Lec 4-1 p. 8, Fig. 5e). The small square stops as a V-pit (self-limited at w/√2); where the bounding rectangles overlap, the mask strip between windows is undercut and the cavities merge.

100.name: Square window along the flat vs at 45° (Paul et al. 2024, Fig. 1a, b)
100.note: Left: edges along ⟨110⟩ (parallel to the flat) give a pit bounded by {111} walls at 54.7° that stops at a V. Right: the same square turned 45° has edges along ⟨100⟩; only {100} planes are exposed, so it etches down and sideways at the same rate with vertical walls and undercuts the mask (Paul et al. 2024, Fig. 1a, b, Sec. I). The paper uses TMAH; here KOH 30 wt% is used because the course files have no full-orientation TMAH rate table (Pal & Sato Table 4.1 is KOH only).

100.name: Membrane pixel with a 45° mask (after Paul et al. 2024, Fig. 1c)
100.note: A square membrane outlined by two L-shaped openings, the whole pattern turned 45° to the flat so that all edges lie along ⟨100⟩ (Paul et al. 2024, Sec. II and Fig. 1c). The {100} side walls undercut the membrane from every trench at about R(100), so it is released from below; it stays held at two opposite corners. This reproduces only the first anisotropic step of Method I (Fig. 3a–c); the HNA isotropic steps are not modelled. Trench width 30 µm and membrane 60 µm are design choices (the paper gives only a 128 × 60 µm mask, Sec. IV); KOH 30 wt% replaces TMAH (no TMAH rate table in the course files).

100.name: Ring window: round island with convex-corner attack
100.note: An annular opening leaves a round island of silicon. Outside, the cavity grows to the ⟨110⟩ square that bounds the ring (concave side, slow {111}); the island edge is convex everywhere, so fast planes eat it and it turns into a polygon (Lec 4-1 p. 8). Ring sizes are design choices.

100.name: Array of small squares at 45° (2 × 3, pitch 90 µm)
100.note: One shape with the array option: 3 × 2 copies at 90 µm pitch. Each 45° square exposes {100} walls and grows sideways at about R(100) until neighbouring cavities meet (Paul et al. 2024, Fig. 1b). Sizes are design choices.

100.name: Cross-shaped window: concave and convex corners
100.note: The four inner corners of the cross are convex silicon corners and are undercut; the outer corners are concave and stay sharp. Given enough time the cavity becomes the bounding square (Lec 4-1 p. 8, Fig. 5e).

100.name: p++ boron etch stop: the pit floor stops on a buried layer (Pal & Sato p. 93)
100.note: A 200 µm window with edges along ⟨110⟩ over a p++ layer with 1 × 10²⁰ cm⁻³ boron, 30 to 33 µm below the surface (3 µm: the depth thermal diffusion reaches in practice, Pal & Sato p. 93). Above the layer the floor moves at R(100) = 0.797 µm/min (Table 4.1, p. 87) and reaches it after 37.6 min; inside it the rate is × 0.022, read from Fig. 4.11 (p. 93), so after 60 min the floor stands at 30.4 µm instead of 47.8 µm, while the {111} walls are unchanged. The layer depth and the use of the Si(100) factor for every plane are assumptions; see “Doping and the p++ etch stop”.

110.name: Parallelogram window: vertical {111} walls (Lec 4-1 p. 12, Fig. 24)
110.note: Window edges along the two vertical-{111} traces (54.74° and 125.26° to a ⟨110⟩ flat). The four long walls are vertical {111}; inclined {111} at 35.26° appear at the acute corners (Lec 4-1 p. 12).

110.name: Parallel trenches with thin walls (Lec 4-1 p. 12, Fig. 25)
110.note: Line patterns along a vertical-{111} trace give deep trenches with vertical walls; the silicon walls between them stay (Lec 4-1 p. 12, Fig. 25 a, b). The trench ends lie along the flat, so inclined {111} planes close them and limit the depth. Design choice: the walls here are 60 µm wide along the flat (49 µm normal to the wall); the grid is capped at 5 µm because the first-order scheme slowly thins walls narrower than about 8 grid cells (numerical, not physical).

110.name: Line along the flat: shallow V-groove (Lec 4-1 p. 12, Fig. 25)
110.note: Lines parallel to the inclined {111} traces give shallow V-grooves with walls at 35.26° (Lec 4-1 p. 12, Fig. 25 caption).

110.name: Circle window, ⟨111⟩ arrow convention (HW2 P5)
110.note: Frame of HW2 P5: the ⟨111⟩ arrow is the outward flat normal, so vertical {111} traces lie parallel to the flat and at 70.53° to it (Flat and Arrow Note, Table 1).

110.name: Cantilever on (110): convex-corner undercut
110.note: A beam with edges along the vertical-{111} traces keeps vertical walls on its sides; it is released from its free end, where the convex corners expose fast planes.

111.name: Pre-etched holes: lateral undercut merges under the mask
111.note: (111) itself barely etches (R(111) = 0.005 µm/min, Pal & Sato p. 87), so the holes are first etched straight down (pre-etch depth is an assumption, e.g. by deep RIE, Lec 4-1 p. 16). KOH then undercuts sideways until inclined {111} planes stop it; neighbouring cavities merge.

111.name: Triangle window, pre-etched 30 µm
111.note: Three walls slope inward and three are undercut, all {111} (Lec 4-1 p. 13, Fig. 7b); the inclined {111} planes make 70.53° with the (111) surface (derived: angle between two {111} normals). Pre-etch depth is an assumption.
